title: Annuity: level cash flows
subtitle: A series of equal payments over a fixed period
openingQuestion: You buy a house on a mortgage of 10 million VND/month for 20 years. What kind of cash flow is this?
openingOptions: There is no special name for this kind of level cash flow at all
Annuity - a series of equal payments over a finite period
explanation: An annuity is a series of equal cash flows repeating over a fixed number of periods - mortgage payments, insurance premiums, and bond coupons all take this shape. The formula PV = PMT × [(1 − (1+r)^−n) / r] is just a shortcut for discounting each period and adding them up. Understanding it answers very practical questions: what a 9 million VND monthly payment over 20 years is actually worth today, and the gap versus the house price is exactly the interest you pay the bank.

realWorldExample.description: Monthly home mortgage loans over 15-20 years are the most common real-life example of an annuity - banks calculate the monthly payment precisely from the PV Annuity formula, so that the present value of all the payments exactly equals the original loan amount.

quiz.question: What is the difference between an annuity due and an ordinary annuity?
options: An annuity due lasts forever, an ordinary annuity has a fixed term
An annuity due has a fixed rate, an ordinary annuity floats
An annuity due pays at the start of each period, an ordinary annuity pays at the end
An annuity due is for businesses, an ordinary annuity is for individuals
quiz.explanation: Ordinary annuity: payment at the end of each period - the most common form (loan payments). Annuity due: payment at the start of each period (rent paid in advance). Because the money arrives sooner, the PV of an annuity due is higher.

quiz.question: A bank raises its mortgage rate. For the same loan amount and term, how does the monthly payment change?
options: It rises, because a fixed PV forces PMT to rise when r rises
It falls, because a higher rate shrinks the present value
It stays the same, because the loan amount and term are unchanged
It can't be determined without knowing the value of the house
quiz.explanation: From PV = PMT × [(1−(1+r)^−n)/r], when PV (the loan amount) and n (the term) are fixed, a rise in r forces PMT to rise to keep the equation balanced - this is why mortgage payments go up when lending rates rise.

quiz.question: Borrow 1 billion VND at 8%/year, repaid evenly over 10 years. Roughly how much is the annual payment?
options: ≈ 149 million/year (total repaid 1.49 billion)
100 million/year (= 1 billion ÷ 10, splitting the principal evenly and ignoring interest)
180 million/year (= 100 + a flat 80 in interest each year)
≈ 108 million/year (= 1.08 billion ÷ 10, one-off interest)
quiz.explanation: PMT = PV × r / [1 − (1+r)^−n] = 1,000 × 0.08 / 0.5368 ≈ 149 million. Total repaid is 1.49 billion, of which 490 million is interest - a figure the naive divide-by-ten approach misses entirely.

quiz.question: Stretching the loan term from 10 years to 20 years, same rate, what happens?
options: The annual payment stays the same, only the term lengthens
Both the annual payment and the total amount repaid fall
The annual payment falls by exactly half, the total stays the same
The annual payment eases but the total amount repaid rises
quiz.explanation: For 1 billion at 8%, ten years means 149 million/year and a 1.49 billion total; twenty years means 102 million/year but a 2.04 billion total. A longer term doesn't make the loan cheaper - it shifts the burden from the monthly cash flow to the total cost.

quiz.question: Why is pricing a coupon bond fundamentally an annuity problem?
options: Because the coupon rate always equals the discount rate exactly
Because bonds are always paid at the start of each period
Because the coupons are a level cash flow, plus the face value at maturity
Because the face value is repaid evenly across the years
quiz.explanation: Bond price = PV of the coupon stream (an annuity) + PV of the face value repaid at maturity. This is why the annuity formula reappears the moment you move into bond valuation.

keyTakeaways: Annuity = a series of equal payments over a fixed period

practicePrompt.question: A retirement insurance policy pays you a level 20 million VND every year, for exactly 15 years, then stops. What kind of cash flow is this, and how does it differ from a cash flow that pays forever?
options: This is an Annuity: a fixed run of level payments, unlike a Perpetuity which simply carries on forever
This is a Perpetuity because the payment amount is the same every year
This isn't a well-defined cash flow structure in finance at all, just a random stream of income
Annuity and Perpetuity are just two different names for the same kind of cash flow
practicePrompt.explanation: Annuity = a series of equal payments over a fixed period (here, 15 years). Unlike a Perpetuity - a level cash flow that continues forever (like a fixed preferred dividend) - an annuity has a clear end date, and its PV formula differs from the perpetuity formula PV = C/r.

summary.keyIdea: Annuity = a series of equal payments over a fixed period
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Calculate the PV of a payment plan
application.message: If you are or have ever considered buying on installments (house, car, insurance), try using the PV Annuity formula to work out the real present value of everything you'll pay.
application.secondary: Many installment plans look cheap but their real PV is higher than you think.

sections.text: An annuity (level cash flow) is a series of equal payments, occurring at regular intervals over a fixed period - from mortgage payments and life insurance premiums to bond coupons. Pricing an annuity is one of the most common practical applications of the time value of money.

PV = PMT × [(1 − (1+r)^−n) / r], where PMT is the payment per period, r is the rate per period, n is the number of periods. **Example:** a bank loan of 1 billion VND, repaid evenly over 10 years, at 8%/year. The bank sets PMT so that the PV of the entire repayment stream exactly equals the original 1 billion loan - this is exactly how the annuity formula is used to compute the annual payment on any loan.

Ordinary annuity: payment at the end of each period - the most common form, applying to most installment loans. Annuity due: payment at the start of each period - for example, rent is usually paid before the month begins. Because the money arrives sooner, the PV of an annuity due is always higher than the PV of an ordinary annuity with the same PMT, r, and n.

example.title: Borrow 1 billion, 8%/year, repaid evenly over 10 years
example.explanation: 490 million in interest on a 1 billion loan. Stretch the term to 20 years and each year drops to just 102 million - much lighter - but the total to repay becomes 2.04 billion. A longer term doesn't make the loan cheaper, it shifts money from the monthly cash flow to the total cost.

left.label: Ordinary annuity
left.text: Paid at the END of each period. Most installment loans take this form. Each payment is discounted one extra period compared to an annuity due.

right.label: Annuity due
right.text: Paid at the START of each period - rent, insurance premiums. PV is higher by exactly a factor of (1+r): the same 8%/year cash flow costs 8% more.

items: A higher lending rate → PMT (the payment) must rise to keep PV = the loan amount unchanged
A longer loan term (larger n) → PMT per period falls, but the total repaid over the loan's life rises
The annuity is the pricing tool for coupon bonds: bond price = PV(coupon annuity) + PV(face value)
Don't confuse an annuity (fixed term) with a perpetuity (goes on forever) - the formulas differ

lines: Every time you make a mortgage payment, a car payment, or pay an insurance premium, you're directly interacting with the PV Annuity formula, even without realizing it.
